title: The Sharpe Pint: Gated Alts, Gilt Tremors, and the Five Sins of Financial AI

opening_mood.text: Morning. Grab a pint—or a very strong espresso, given the state of the screens. If you thought the summer doldrums were setting in, yesterday's market action had other ideas. We have got a global tech bath, private credit gates slamming shut, a gravity check for Elon, and a UK political coup. Let's get into it.

content.text: If you thought the summer lull was kicking in, think again. Yesterday's market action was a proper wake-up call, featuring a global tech rout, private credit gating, a reality check for Elon, and a political earthquake in Westminster.
1. The Great AI & Chip Reality Check: Global Semis Take a Bath

Tech stocks took a proper beating on Tuesday, with the Nasdaq falling 2.2% and the S&P 500 dropping 1.4% as a global rout in technology and chipmaker stocks deepened. The pain was felt worldwide: South Korea's KOSPI plummeted nearly 10%, triggering an automatic trading halt as overseas investors dumped chip heavyweights Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, which both tumbled over 12%. In the US, memory giant Micron Technology lost 13.2% and Nvidia fell 4.1%.

Why it matters: The market is finally asking the hard question: are hyperscalers overspending on AI infrastructure without a clear path to monetisation? If software revenues do not start justifying the massive hardware capex, the valuation multiple compression across the entire semiconductor supply chain could be severe.

The City angle: For asset managers and quant funds, this is a classic momentum reversal. The extreme concentration in AI-related semis means that when the music stops, index-level drawdowns are brutal. In interviews or client meetings, this is a great opportunity to discuss the transition from 'infrastructure build' to 'application monetisation' in the AI cycle.
2. Apollo Gates Its Flagship Private Credit Fund as Redemptions Surge

Apollo Global Management has capped withdrawals from its $26 billion retail-focused private credit fund, Apollo Debt Solutions (ADS), at the standard 5% limit. This came after investors requested to redeem a massive 16.8% (roughly $2.4 billion) of outstanding shares in Q2, up from 11.2% in Q1. This marks the second consecutive quarter of gating for Apollo's flagship retail vehicle, highlighting the structural liquidity mismatch of 'semi-liquid' funds.

Why it matters: Apollo is not alone; firms like Cliffwater and BlackRock have also faced double-digit redemption requests and enforced similar caps recently. The anxiety is driven by private credit's heavy exposure to software buyouts, where business models are perceived as highly vulnerable to AI disruption. Interestingly, there is a stark regional split: US onshore redemption requests moderated to 4.3%, while offshore (international) requests surged to 12.5%.

The City angle: This story is gold dust for interviews in private markets or asset management. It perfectly illustrates the 'liquidity mismatch'—offering quarterly redemptions on highly illiquid, direct-lent mid-market corporate loans. While Apollo points to robust institutional demand to offset retail outflows, the retail 'wealth channel' is clearly showing signs of fatigue.
3. SpaceX's Post-IPO Gravity Check: $1 Trillion Wiped in Three Days

After its historic $75 billion Nasdaq debut on June 12 at $150 per share—which briefly pushed its valuation past $2.5 trillion and made Elon Musk the world's first trillionaire—SpaceX (SPCX) has suffered a brutal reality check. Shares briefly fell below their debut price to $149 on Tuesday before recovering slightly to close at $156. The three-day losing streak has wiped nearly $1 trillion off the company's peak market value.

Why it matters: The selloff accelerated after SpaceX launched a massive $20 billion senior bond sale to fund AI data centres and repay a bridge loan. While the company has a massive $100.8 billion cash pile, the sudden debt issuance spooked equity investors who realized that even a $2 trillion rocket company has massive, capital-intensive capex requirements. It proves that public markets will eventually demand a path to self-sustaining cash flows rather than endless capex.

The City angle: This is a classic 'buy the rumour, sell the fact' IPO. The massive retail allocation (30% of the float) meant the initial pop was highly retail-driven. Now, institutional reality is setting in, and anyone who bought after the first day of trading is officially underwater. It also raises serious questions about the pricing of upcoming mega-IPOs like OpenAI and Anthropic.
4. Cerebras Beats on Earnings but Gets Punished on Margins

AI chipmaker Cerebras Systems (CBRS), which raised $6.4 billion in May in the largest semiconductor IPO of all time, reported its first quarterly earnings. Core revenue jumped 92% to $191.3 million, beating estimates, and they announced a massive multi-year deal with OpenAI for 750MW of compute valued at over $20 billion. Despite the beat, the stock plunged over 10% in after-hours trading.

Why it matters: The devil is in the margins. Cerebras projected full-year negative margins and its gross margins remain well below those of AI chip rivals like Nvidia. Challenging the king of GPUs is an expensive business, and the market is realising that wafer-scale engines are incredibly costly to manufacture.

The City angle: This is a classic 'revenue growth vs. profitability' battle. For tech bankers and growth equity investors, Cerebras is the ultimate test case of whether a startup can realistically break Nvidia's monopoly, or if the capital intensity of doing so will destroy shareholder value.
5. UK Political Earthquake: Starmer Resigns, Burnham Poised for No. 10

Keir Starmer has resigned as Prime Minister after just two years in office, bowing to intense pressure over the economy and internal Labour discontent. Andy Burnham, the 'King of the North' and former Mayor of Greater Manchester, is the runaway favourite to succeed him, running virtually unopposed after potential rival Darren Jones ruled himself out.

Why it matters: Burnham would be the UK's seventh Prime Minister in a decade. Tensions are incredibly high, with Starmer and Burnham holding a 'frosty' meeting to thrash out a transition of power. Markets are highly sensitive to who Burnham will choose as his Chancellor, with rumours that Rachel Reeves may be replaced.

The City angle: For gilt traders and sterling strategists, political stability is paramount. Darren Jones' warning to Burnham not to veer too far to the left on economic policy is exactly what the City is worried about. A shift toward more interventionist, northern-focused economic policies could pressure gilts if it implies higher spending.
6. FedEx Beats Estimates but Tumbles on Outlook and Post-Spin 'Stranded Costs'
Logistics giant FedEx (FDX) reported strong Q4 results, with adjusted EPS of $6.31 on $25 billion in revenue, beating Wall Street estimates. However, the stock fell over 6% in after-hours trading.

Why it matters: Investors are spooked by the company's calendar year 2026 outlook and the 'stranded costs' left behind by the recently completed spin-off of its FedEx Freight unit on June 1. Additionally, cost pressures from a new pilot contract and shifting global trade flows due to tariffs and the war in Iran are weighing on margins.

The City angle: FedEx is the ultimate global economic barometer. While its cost-saving 'Network 2.0' initiative is progressing (now handling 45% of eligible volume), the muted package demand and margin pressure suggest that global trade remains sluggish.

sections.title: Markets Briefing: What Moved and Why

content.text: Let's unpack what is actually going on behind the screens. Global markets just got a double-shot of espresso, courtesy of a brutal tech sell-off, a shocking hawkish pivot from Bank of America, and some serious plumbing issues in the private credit space.
The Tech Rout: AI Jitters and a Korean Trading Halt

On Tuesday, the S&P 500 slid 1.4% to 7,365.46 and the tech-heavy Nasdaq tumbled 2.2% to 25,587.04. The carnage started overnight in Seoul, where South Korea’s Kospi index plunged a staggering 10%—triggering a temporary trading halt—as chip heavyweights Samsung and SK Hynix both cratered by over 12%. The contagion quickly crossed the Pacific. Micron Technology sank 13.2%, Sandisk dropped over 13%, and Nvidia shed 4.1%.

What is driving this? It is a classic case of the 'show me the money' phase of the AI cycle. Investors are starting to ask hard questions about the eye-watering capital expenditure being poured into AI infrastructure and whether the near-term enterprise demand actually justifies these valuations. While the Kospi staged a 3.3% rebound on Wednesday morning (with Samsung clawing back 9.8%), the underlying message is clear: the easy-money momentum trade in semiconductors is hitting a wall of volatility.
The Macro Shock: BofA Drops a Hawkish Hammer

But tech was not acting in a vacuum. The real macro hand grenade was lobbed by Bank of America’s research team on Monday. In a stunning reversal, BofA scrapped its softer rate outlook and now projects three consecutive 25-basis-point rate hikes this year—in September, October, and December—which would lift the Fed funds rate to 4.25%–4.50%. Deutsche Bank quickly followed suit, penciling in two hikes.

This hawkish pivot is a direct reaction to the regime shift under the new Fed Chair, Kevin Warsh, who took the gavel in May. At his debut FOMC meeting last week, Warsh kept rates steady at 3.5%–3.75% but delivered a remarkably hawkish presser, cutting the official statement to a blunt 114 words and signaling that the Fed is shifting from 'risk management' to 'supply shock management'. With core inflation remaining sticky and the US 10-year Treasury yield holding near 4.5%, the market is suddenly realising that the next move from the central bank might be a squeeze, not a pause.
Private Credit: Gated Communities

Meanwhile, in the shadows of the private markets, the plumbing is starting to rattle. Apollo Global Management has capped quarterly redemptions at 5% for its flagship $26 billion retail private credit fund, Apollo Debt Solutions (ADS). Why? Because a massive 16.8% ($2.4 billion) of the fund's shares were put up for redemption in Q2, up from 11.2% in Q1.

This is a classic mismatch: offering semi-liquid, quarterly exit doors to retail investors on highly illiquid private loans. It is not just Apollo, either—Blackstone and Cliffwater have also had to cap redemptions recently. Underneath the hood, investors are increasingly nervous about private credit’s heavy exposure to software companies, whose business models look highly vulnerable to AI disruption. As one advisor put it, 2026 is turning out to be the year the semi-liquid alts plumbing gets thoroughly tested.
SpaceX: Debt is Harder Than Equity

Finally, Elon Musk’s SpaceX provided a fascinating case study in cross-asset pricing. Fresh off its blockbuster IPO earlier this month, the rocket and satellite giant priced its debut $25 billion bond sale on Tuesday. While it drew a massive $89 billion in orders, bond investors proved to be a much tougher crowd than equity bulls. SpaceX had to offer relatively generous yields—about 1.4 percentage points above comparable Treasuries for its 10-year tranche—to compensate for its massive projected cash burn. SpaceX shares fell 16% on Monday and remained highly volatile, showing that even the most hyped AI and space plays are not immune to the gravity of the corporate bond market.

content.text: Financial Idea of the Day: The Gross Profitability Premium (And Why the Bottom Line Lies)

If you’ve spent any time in equity research, asset management, or prepping for finance interviews, you’ve probably had "Quality" beaten into your head. Buy high-quality businesses. Look for high Return on Equity (ROE), high Return on Assets (ROA), or fat net margins. But there’s a massive, structural flaw with looking at the bottom line to judge how good a business actually is: the accounting rules are actively trying to mislead you.

Enter Robert Novy-Marx, a finance professor at the University of Rochester. In 2013, he published a landmark paper called "The Other Side of Value: The Gross Profitability Premium". His thesis was simple but punchy: the cleanest, most predictive measure of a company’s true economic productivity isn't net income or free cash flow. It’s Gross Profit divided by Total Assets. And companies that score highly on this metric absolutely trounce the market.
The Intuition: Why the Top of the P&L Rules

Why does gross profit (Revenue minus Cost of Goods Sold) beat net income? Because net income is noisy. It gets dragged down by interest expenses, tax structures, and—most importantly—investments in growth that are forced to run through the income statement rather than the balance sheet. Under standard accounting rules (like US GAAP or IFRS), when a company builds a physical factory, it capitalises the cost on the balance sheet. But when a company builds an intangible asset—like a brand through marketing, or software through R&D—it has to expense those costs immediately on the P&L. This artificially depresses net income, making a brilliant, high-growth business look like a dog on a standard ROA or ROE screen.

Gross profit ignores all that noise. It tells you whether the core product or service actually has a structural edge. If a company can generate massive gross profits relative to the assets it employs, it has a highly productive economic engine. How it chooses to spend those profits (whether on R&D, aggressive marketing, or just letting it drop to the bottom line) is a secondary capital allocation decision.
A Tale of Two Firms
Let’s look at a simple example. Imagine two UK tech firms, both with £100m in total assets:

items: Company A (The Compounder): Generates £40m in revenue with £10m in COGS, leaving £30m in Gross Profit. It’s growing fast, so it spends £25m on R&D and marketing. Net Income is £5m.
Company B (The Legacy Slogger): Generates £40m in revenue with £30m in COGS, leaving £10m in Gross Profit. It spends just £5m on basic admin. Net Income is £5m.

content.text: If you run a basic quantitative screen looking at Return on Assets (Net Income / Assets), both companies look identical at a mediocre 5% (£5m / £100m). But look at their Gross Profitability (Gross Profit / Assets):

Company A has a vastly superior business model. Its 'low' net income is a deliberate choice to reinvest in the business. Company B is structurally weak; its low gross margin means it has zero pricing power and is highly vulnerable to cost inflation. Over a multi-year horizon, Company A’s stock is highly likely to outperform Company B’s.
Why Asset Managers Care: The Value Hedge

In quantitative finance and asset management, the Gross Profitability Premium is often called "the other side of value". Traditional value investing (buying low price-to-book or low P/E stocks) works, but it can expose you to "value traps"—cheap companies that are cheap because they are dying. Highly profitable companies, on the other hand, tend to trade at higher valuations (growth stocks).

Novy-Marx showed that because gross profitability and value are highly complementary, combining them is an absolute cheat code. Profitable growth companies act as a perfect hedge for cheap value companies. When value is getting hammered, your high-gross-profitability growth names carry the portfolio, and vice versa. It’s why giants like Dimensional Fund Advisors (DFA) and AQR immediately integrated this metric into their core systematic strategies.
The Common Beginner Mistake

The classic mistake is relying on EBITDA or Net Income margins to screen for "quality" without adjusting for business model differences. If you screen out companies with low net margins, you will systematically miss early-stage compounders that are expensing their growth. Conversely, if you only look at high-margin legacy businesses, you might end up buying capital-intensive operations that require massive capex just to stay in place.
How to Use This in an Interview

If an interviewer asks you: "How do you define a high-quality business?" or "What is your favourite financial metric?", do not just say "ROIC" or "high margins" like everyone else. Stand out by bringing up the Gross Profitability Premium:

"While most people look at ROIC or net margins to judge quality, I like to look at Gross Profit to Total Assets. It’s a concept popularized by Robert Novy-Marx. By looking at the very top of the P&L relative to the asset base, you strip out the noise of capital structure, taxes, and—crucially—the accounting distortion where growth investments like R&D and marketing are expensed rather than capitalised. It lets you see the true economic productivity of the business engine before management decides how to reinvest those profits."
Over a Pint

Next time you're debating stock picks with colleagues or mates at the pub, you can sum it up like this: "Gross profit to assets tells you if the engine actually works. Net income just tells you how much fuel they decided to burn this year."

sections.title: Quant / AI Finance Idea of the Day

content.text: If you’ve ever tried to train a deep learning model to manage a global macro portfolio, you’ve probably run straight into the three horsemen of the quant apocalypse: look-ahead bias from asynchronous market closes, a signal-to-noise ratio that makes a dial-up modem sound clear, and a model that looks like a genius in backtests but folds like a cheap tent the moment a new market regime hits.

A brilliant paper from the Oxford-Man Institute of Quantitative Finance, titled "DeePM: Regime-Robust Deep Learning for Systematic Macro Portfolio Management" (published in January 2026 by Kieran Wood, Stephen J. Roberts, and Stefan Zohren), introduces a structured deep-learning portfolio manager that tackles these exact real-world headaches head-on. It offers a masterclass in how to inject economic structure and risk-robustness into neural networks.
The Ragged Filtration Problem & The Causal Sieve

Let's start with a classic trap: the "ragged filtration" problem. Global markets don't close at the same time. Tokyo closes hours before London, which closes before New York. If you feed daily closing prices into a standard cross-sectional attention layer (like a Transformer), the model will happily let Tokyo's trading signal "attend" to New York's close on the same calendar day. Congratulations, you’ve accidentally built a time machine. Your model is trading Japanese equities using future US data that didn't exist when Tokyo closed.

To fix this, the authors introduce the Directed Delay (or Causal Sieve). It strictly lags cross-sectional conditioning based on actual local closing times. Tokyo can only attend to New York's previous day's close, while New York can attend to Tokyo's same-day close. It prioritises causal, real-world information flow over naive "freshness."
Regularising with a Macroeconomic Graph Prior

Financial data is notoriously noisy. If you let a Graph Neural Network (GNN) try to learn the relationships between 50 different global assets from scratch, it will end up fitting to statistical noise and trading ghosts. DeePM solves this by injecting a Macroeconomic Graph Prior—a structural map of the world based on economic first principles (e.g., linking oil to inflation, or interest rates to currencies). The GNN is forced to respect these fundamental pathways, keeping its search space disciplined and economically grounded.
The Smooth Worst-Window Penalty (EVaR Proxy)

Most portfolio models are trained to maximise the average Sharpe ratio over the entire training set. The problem? The optimiser will happily find a policy that crushes it during a multi-year bull run (like the 2010s) even if it completely blows up during a crisis (like 2020). In the real world, that gets you fired.

DeePM swaps this out for a distributionally robust objective using a smooth worst-window penalty. It splits the historical returns into rolling windows (e.g., 1-year periods), calculates the Sharpe ratio for each, and applies a SoftMin function. By minimising this SoftMin loss, the model is forced to focus on improving its worst-performing periods. It’s a differentiable proxy for Entropic Value-at-Risk (EVaR), ensuring the strategy is built to survive the worst storms, not just cruise in fair weather.
Python Implementation: Smooth Worst-Window Sharpe Loss

import torch

def smooth_worst_window_sharpe(returns, window_size=252, step_size=21, temperature=1.0):
    """
    Computes a differentiable proxy for Entropic Value-at-Risk (EVaR)
    by applying a SoftMin over rolling window Sharpe ratios.
    """
    T = returns.shape[0]
    window_sharpes = []
    
    # Extract rolling windows
    for start in range(0, T - window_size + 1, step_size):
        window_ret = returns[start : start + window_size]
        mean = torch.mean(window_ret)
        std = torch.max(torch.std(window_ret), torch.tensor(1e-6))
        # Annualised Sharpe ratio (assuming daily returns)
        sharpe = (mean / std) * torch.sqrt(torch.tensor(252.0))
        window_sharpes.append(sharpe)
        
    window_sharpes = torch.stack(window_sharpes)
    
    # SoftMin over window Sharpe ratios to penalise the worst-performing windows
    # SoftMin(x) = Sum(x_i * exp(-x_i / temp)) / Sum(exp(-x_i / temp))
    weights = torch.softmax(-window_sharpes / temperature, dim=0)
    smooth_worst_sharpe = torch.sum(window_sharpes * weights)
    
    # We want to maximise this, so the loss to minimise is its negative
    return -smooth_worst_sharpe
Over a Pint: How to Use This in an Interview or at Work

items: The "Time Machine" Trap: If you're interviewing for a systematic macro role, bring up the ragged filtration problem. Ask: "How do you handle cross-sectional attention across global time zones without leaking future US closes into Asian signals?" It shows you actually understand the plumbing of real-world data, not just toy datasets.

Differentiable Risk Measures: If someone talks about optimising portfolios for Value-at-Risk (VaR) or Expected Shortfall (ES), point out that these are notoriously difficult to use in gradient descent because they are non-differentiable. Explain how a SoftMin over rolling window Sharpe ratios acts as a smooth, differentiable proxy for Entropic Value-at-Risk (EVaR).

Economic Priors vs. Pure ML: In a debate about "pure data-driven" vs. "hand-crafted" models, argue that pure ML in finance is a fool's errand due to low signal-to-noise. The winning play is hybrid: using a macroeconomic graph prior to regularise a GNN, forcing the AI to respect basic economic gravity.

sections.title: One Article or Paper Worth Reading

content.text: If you’ve spent any time on financial Twitter, LinkedIn, or reading tech blogs lately, you’ll have seen a dozen papers claiming that ChatGPT or some custom LLM can generate 40% annualised returns by reading earnings transcripts. It sounds amazing. It also, in about 99% of cases, is absolute bollocks.

A brilliant paper published in February 2026 takes a sledgehammer to this hype. It is called "Evaluating LLMs in Finance Requires Explicit Bias Consideration" by Yaxuan Kong, Stefan Zohren, Alejandro Lopez-Lira, and a team of researchers from Oxford, Florida, and other top institutions. It is the ultimate BS-detector for the AI era.
Why This Paper Matters

The authors did something simple but devastating: they reviewed 164 academic and industry papers published between 2023 and 2025 that claimed to use LLMs for financial tasks (like trading, sentiment analysis, or forecasting). They checked if these papers followed basic, first-year quant finance rules. Spoiler alert: they didn't. The authors identified what they call the "Five Sins" of financial LLM evaluation, showing how easily researchers fool themselves into thinking they've found alpha when they've actually just found a new way to cheat.
The Five Sins of Financial LLMs

items: Look-Ahead Bias (The Time-Traveler): This is the big one. It happens in two ways. First, 'Parametric Knowledge Leakage'—if you backtest an LLM on 2023 data, but the model was pre-trained on internet data up to 2024, the model already knows who won the Super Bowl and which tech stocks rallied. Second, 'External Knowledge Leakage'—using a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system that pulls from a database or live search that has been updated with post-event information.

Survivorship Bias (The Ghost Town): Evaluating an LLM's stock-picking ability historically using only the companies currently in the S&P 500. It completely ignores the companies that went bankrupt or were delisted along the way. Shockingly, only 1.2% of the 164 papers reviewed even acknowledged this basic error.

Narrative Bias (The Storyteller): LLMs are designed to be coherent and persuasive. They will generate highly plausible-sounding investment theses that are completely unsupported by hard financial reality, creating an 'illusion of understanding' that masks underlying complexity.

Objective Bias (The Confident Guesser): LLMs are trained to predict the next token and be helpful, not to maximise Sharpe ratios. They are structurally biased toward confident guessing and hallucinating certainty rather than admitting ignorance or abstaining when the data is noisy.

Cost Bias (The Margin Killer): Ignoring transaction costs, bid-ask slippage, and—crucially—API inference costs. A high-frequency sentiment trading strategy might look profitable on paper, but if calling GPT-4 or Claude 3.5 Opus 10,000 times a day costs more than the alpha you generate, you're just subsidising Big Tech.

content.text: Key Quotes
"Finance-specific biases can inflate performance, contaminate backtests, and make reported results useless for any deployment claim."
"We reviewed 164 papers... and found that no single bias is discussed in more than 28 percent of studies."
How to Read It

You don't need to get bogged down in the heavy mathematical formalisations of the biases or the detailed breakdown of the 164 papers. Skim those. Instead, focus on Section 3, which defines the Five Sins, and Section 4, where they introduce their 'Structural Validity Framework' and a practical checklist for evaluating any financial LLM system.
How This Connects to You

If you are a junior or mid-level analyst, quant, or PM, you are going to be pitched 'AI-driven' tools, either by external vendors or over-enthusiastic internal developers. This paper gives you the exact questions to ask to tear those pitches apart. If you are interviewing for a quant or asset management role, bringing up 'parametric knowledge leakage in LLM backtesting' shows you understand both cutting-edge AI and classic, rigorous financial engineering. It immediately separates you from the crowd of people who just prompt ChatGPT to write Python scripts.
What to Say at the Pub or in a Meeting

items: "Most of these academic papers claiming LLMs can beat the market are just parametric knowledge leakage in disguise—the model was trained on the future and backtested on the past."
"If your LLM trading agent doesn't explicitly factor in API inference costs alongside bid-ask slippage, you aren't trading alpha; you're just running an expensive charity for OpenAI."

"It's wild that only 1.2% of financial LLM papers in the last three years even mentioned survivorship bias. We're applying 21st-century neural networks to data, but forgetting 20th-century basic statistics."

content.text: Our Take

This paper is a much-needed cold shower for the 'AI in finance' hype. The reality is that the laws of quantitative finance are immutable. It doesn't matter if your model has eight billion parameters or eighty trillion; if you feed it future data, ignore transaction costs, or only test it on companies that survived, your backtest is a work of fiction. Before you allocate a single pound to an LLM-driven strategy, make sure it passes the Oxford-Florida structural validity checklist.

content.text: The Streetlight Effect: Why we look where the light is, not where the keys are

Picture this: You’re walking home from a pub in Bank at 1 AM, and you spot a bloke on his hands and knees under a lamppost. You ask him what he’s lost. "My house keys," he says. You help him look for ten minutes. Nothing. Finally, you ask, "Are you sure you dropped them here?" He replies, "No, I dropped them over there in the dark alleyway, but the light is much better over here."

This is the Streetlight Effect (or the "Drunkard’s Search"), a term popularised by philosopher Abraham Kaplan in 1964. It’s the cognitive bias where we look for answers in the easiest, most visible places, rather than where the actual truth is hiding. In the modern, data-drenched City, we are constantly guilty of mistaking "measurable" for "important."
Why it matters in finance

In investing and corporate finance, the streetlight is incredibly bright. It is ridiculously easy to pull historical P/E ratios, EBITDA margins, or beta from a Bloomberg terminal. It’s clean, it’s structured, and it fits beautifully into a PowerPoint slide. But the actual drivers of a company's future—like whether the CEO is a toxic micromanager, if their proprietary tech is actually just three offshore contractors using ChatGPT, or if their supply chain is one geopolitical hiccup away from collapse—are messy and hard to quantify.

So, what do we do? We ignore the dark alleyway. We build a massive, 50-row DCF model projected to four decimal places based entirely on the easily accessible, historical numbers. We mistake precision for accuracy. It’s the financial equivalent of looking for your keys under the lamppost because the Excel gridlines are so beautifully aligned. We see this in ESG too: it’s easy to measure board diversity percentages or carbon emissions scopes (the streetlight), but incredibly hard to measure actual corporate culture or systemic supply chain ethics. Consequently, billions of pounds get allocated based on easily gamified vanity metrics while the real risks remain in the dark.
How to use this at work
To stand out in meetings, interviews, or investment committees, you need to be the person who points into the dark. Here’s how:

items: Ask the "unmeasurable" question: When a colleague presents a highly polished model, ask: "What is the single most important variable we’ve left out of this model simply because we couldn't find a clean data point for it?"

Beware of vanity metrics: If you’re pitching a project or a startup, don't just show "user signups" or "website traffic" because they look good on a chart. Focus on the harder-to-track metrics like actual retention or unit economics.

Do the "dark alley" research: Spend 20% of your research time on qualitative, messy work. Talk to former employees, call up suppliers, or read obscure industry forums. That’s where the keys actually are.

content.text: One line to remember
Don't let a beautiful spreadsheet blind you to a messy reality.
